link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28290.reader_title: Compute allocation records measure reservation, not useful work done
link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28290.reader_what: Allocation records capture occupancy rather than utilisation, so productive value cannot currently be assessed.
link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28290.reader_why: Unmanaged federation can concentrate load and harm on receiving systems while lowering average delay.
link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28290.reader_more: This preprint studies how scarce computing is allocated across federated digital research infrastructure, combining a landscape review of UK and international practice including EuroHPC, a mechanism-design model of allocation under strategic user reports, and simulation on a public workload trace. Three findings recur. First, allocation records measure occupancy, meaning resources reserved, rather than utilisation, meaning useful work done, so funders cannot currently answer whether resources deliver productive value. Second, simple transparent scheduling heuristics perform close to a full-information benchmark once tuned, so the near-term opportunity is instrumenting existing schedulers rather than replacing them. Third, unmanaged federation behaves like uncoordinated routing, minimising average delay while concentrating load on receiving systems, analogous to Braess's paradox in road networks.

deep_analysis.research_question: How scarce compute should be allocated across federated digital research infrastructure, and whether current allocation practice can demonstrate productive value.
deep_analysis.main_finding: Allocation records track occupancy rather than utilisation so productive value is unmeasurable; tuned simple heuristics approach an offline benchmark; and unmanaged federation can concentrate load harmfully while reducing average delay.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Landscape review of UK and international allocation practice with stakeholder survey, a mechanism-design model, and simulation on the public Fresco/Anvil workload trace plus synthetic stress tests.

deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Bears on whether European public compute investment can be shown to deliver research value, a question EuroHPC faces directly.

legacy_versions.reader_what: Digital intensity predicts AI adoption most strongly, with large firms ahead but eastern member states catching up fastest.
legacy_versions.reader_why: Convergence tests indicate narrowing cross-country disparities in AI diffusion across the EU.
legacy_versions.reader_more: This paper examines what determines AI adoption among manufacturing and service enterprises across the 27 EU member states, using a balanced panel combining Eurostat's enterprise ICT usage survey, the Digital Intensity Index and the Community Innovation Survey across two waves in 2023 and 2025. Digital infrastructure emerges as the strongest predictor, with the Digital Intensity Index showing a significant positive effect across pooled, random-effects and fixed-effects specifications. Large firms consistently report higher adoption than smaller ones. Central and Eastern European countries still lag Western Europe but record the fastest growth, with Romania showing a 223 percent increase. Tests of sigma and beta convergence indicate narrowing disparities, which the author reads as a catching-up process in AI diffusion across the Union.

link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s44498-026-.reader_more: This study proposes a framework for evaluating policy in material flow analysis under deep uncertainty, motivated by the observation that conventional uncertainty methods can overstate available knowledge when data is scarce, characterising uncertainty beyond what the evidence supports. The proposed shift is away from identifying the most probable outcomes and towards identifying policies that remain reliable despite uncertainty, achieved by integrating material flow analysis with exploratory modelling that spans broad plausible ranges including extreme scenarios and assesses performance across multiple robustness metrics. The paper also offers technical solutions for handling the constraint that transfer coefficients must sum to one. An illustrative case study demonstrates the framework under simplified conditions, and the authors state further work is needed before systematic application.

deep_analysis.research_question: How to evaluate policy robustly in material flow analysis when data scarcity produces deep uncertainty.
deep_analysis.main_finding: The authors propose replacing most-probable-outcome analysis with robustness-based evaluation across broad plausible uncertainty ranges, and supply methods for handling the sum-to-one constraint on transfer coefficients.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Integration of material flow analysis with exploratory modelling and analysis, demonstrated through an illustrative simplified case study.
deep_analysis.qualification: The authors state explicitly that the case study is illustrative under simplified conditions and that further research is needed before systematic practical application.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Method contribution on reasoning about policy under deep uncertainty, applicable to foresight beyond material flows.

link:https://doi.org/10.1093/forestry/cp.reader_more: Building on a 2022 national horizon scan that identified catastrophic forest ecosystem collapse as the most pressing emerging issue, this paper asks how AI could strengthen foresight and policy coherence in United Kingdom forestry. They propose a six-stage framework combining AI-enabled signal detection with expert interpretation and deliberation: framing, signal discovery, expert engagement, synthesis, simulation and reflexive learning, operationalising responsible research and AI principles. They also advance a forestry foresight lab linking government, research and landowners through federated data commons.

link:https://doi.org/10.34190/eckm.27.1..reader_more: This paper presents an eight-role multi-agent system that turns disclosed patent filings plus a free-text intelligence request into a structured competitive intelligence report. Six frontier models execute the generative roles in parallel, while an independent pool of different models operates verifier, telemetry and judge roles, preserving the principle that the model evaluating an output is never the one that produced it. Evaluation covers four heterogeneous patent filings, reporting per-model precision, recall, semantic alignment and calibration error alongside cost and elapsed time.

legacy_versions.reader_more: The analysis covers initiatives across all major regions and five domains, showing that EU external digital action now extends well beyond regulation into infrastructure, research, cybersecurity and security cooperation. link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24879.reader_title: Framework for governing generative AI in research where private and social returns diverge
link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24879.reader_what: Generative AI raises individual research output while risking collective harms, so the authors propose four governance principles.
link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24879.reader_why: Builds on existing EU AI Act scaffolding to address risks individual researchers cannot observe or manage.
link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24879.reader_more: The paper maps disagreement in the research community across four stages: funding, research tasks, publication and peer review, and use and uptake. It reports that evidence for productivity, augmentation and democratisation has strengthened, but that the picture changes once productivity is disaggregated: gains appear in publication volume and citation share, while evidence on novelty, disruption and breakthrough output is ambiguous or negative. Three mechanisms are said to separate private from social returns: information asymmetry, negative externalities on the shared knowledge base, and depletion of research capacity. The proposed response, Responsible Research with AI, sets out disclosure, differentiation, narrative and proportionality. It is a preprint built on a roundtable and existing literature.

deep_analysis.research_question: How should research systems govern generative AI when individual gains and collective costs diverge?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Proposes a four-principle governance framework matched to three distinct mechanisms separating private from social returns.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Synthesis of an academic roundtable and a fast-expanding empirical literature
deep_analysis.qualification: Preprint, not peer reviewed; the framework is proposed rather than tested, and evidence on novelty effects remains contested.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns governance of AI within the European research system and builds on the EU AI Act.

Between 2014 and 2023 the scheme funded 1,731 projects across 30 EU and associated countries, an investment of €259 million. Health biotechnology and medical technology account for 43 per cent of the portfolio, followed by advanced materials at 17 per cent, artificial intelligence and information technology at 13 per cent and quantum technologies at 12 per cent. The patenting comparison does not adjust for the fact that grantees apply and are selected competitively.

link:https://fiia.fi/wp-content/uploads/.reader_title: Four scenarios for Europe's growth model in an age of strategic capitalism
link:https://fiia.fi/wp-content/uploads/.reader_what: Paper argues the EU's growth model relies on externally sourced inputs and technologies, leaving it structurally fragile.
link:https://fiia.fi/wp-content/uploads/.reader_more: Strategic capitalism here describes an environment in which industrial policy, investment screening and export controls have become ordinary instruments of statecraft. The authors argue that Europe's current model, built on externally sourced inputs, technologies and infrastructures, is fragile under those conditions, and that its innovation future depends on aligning competitiveness with control over critical economic flows and a clear direction for innovation. They set out four trajectories: Dependent Europe, innovation without control or direction; Fortress Europe, control without dynamism; Fragmented Europe, ambition without alignment; and Strategic Europe, which aligns all three and is the only one they see leading to sustained technological leadership. The scenarios are analytical constructions used to structure the argument rather than predictions.

deep_analysis.qualification: Scenario-based argument rather than empirical modelling, so the trajectories illustrate possibilities and are not forecasts. Note that the package's scanner metadata names a different author; the paper itself is by Mikael Wigell and Sinikukka Saari.

link:https://doi.org/10.1080/00343404.20.reader_title: Mapping where AI is invented, encountered and actually used across European regions
link:https://doi.org/10.1080/00343404.20.reader_what: Exposure and worker use are widespread, while invention and firm adoption stay concentrated in wealthy, high-skill hubs.
link:https://doi.org/10.1080/00343404.20.reader_why: Authors call for place-sensitive policy: support leading regions while building capability in lagging ones.
link:https://doi.org/10.1080/00343404.20.reader_more: The study uses six indicators across EU NUTS-2 regions, the statistical unit roughly equivalent to a province or large region, to separate three distinct things: where AI is invented, where workers and industries are exposed to it, and where it is actually used. The pattern the authors call a spatial paradox is that exposure and individual use spread fairly broadly while invention and firm-level adoption cluster in regions with high income and highly educated workforces. They describe a persistent implementation gap between structural exposure and productive use, attributed to institutional, organisational and capability frictions. Income and human capital track AI activity closely, while trade openness runs the other way. These are associations across regions, not causal estimates.

deep_analysis.research_question: How are AI innovation, exposure and use distributed across European regions, and what regional characteristics are associated with each?
deep_analysis.main_finding: A spatial paradox: AI exposure and worker-level use are relatively widespread across EU regions while innovation and firm-level adoption remain concentrated in high-GDP, human-capital-intensive hubs, leaving a persistent implementation gap between exposure and productive use driven by institutional, organisational and capability frictions.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Six complementary indicators of AI innovation, exposure and use mapped and correlated across EU NUTS-2 regions. Package contained no source text (publisher returned 403), so the abstract was recovered online from the publisher record and the JRC repository entry.
deep_analysis.qualification: Descriptive and correlational rather than causal; indicators are drawn from different reference years, and the authors state the views are their own and not an official European Commission position. Interpretation here rests on the abstract, not the full text.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Provides regional-level evidence on European AI capability and adoption gaps, directly relevant to place-based innovation and cohesion policy.

link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40821-026-.reader_title: Corporate research units patent more green technology when the surrounding region already does
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40821-026-.reader_what: Across 118 European regions, host-region green innovation intensity predicts more green patents by resident corporate research units.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40821-026-.reader_why: Policy implication: attracting R&D investment strengthens regional green knowledge bases and cumulative technological capabilities.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40821-026-.reader_more: The sample covers 231 leading corporate research spenders with inventive activity spread across 118 European regions between 2000 and 2018. Using fixed-effects logistic and Poisson models, with a control function approach to address reverse causation, the authors find that higher green innovation intensity in a host region is associated with both whether and how many green patents the local research unit files. The association holds only under specific conditions: the host region is foreign to the firm, lies in Europe's core, is environmentally polluting, and regulates more strictly than the firm's home country. Knowledge in the region itself, rather than activity in neighbouring regions, drives the pattern. Patents measure inventive output imperfectly and the data end in 2018.

deep_analysis.research_question: Does green knowledge embedded in a host region shape the green innovation of multinational R&D units located there?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Host-region green innovation intensity is significantly associated with both the occurrence and the count of green patents from resident corporate R&D units, indicating reverse technological spillovers from local context into corporate research, but only where the region is foreign, core, environmentally brown and more strictly regulated than the firm's home country.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Two-step econometric strategy with conditional fixed-effects logistic and Poisson models plus a control function approach and robustness checks, on 231 top R&D firms across 118 European regions, 2000-2018; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Results are conditional on specific host-region characteristics, rest on patents as an imperfect proxy for innovation, and remain observational despite endogeneity corrections; data end in 2018.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Bears on whether attracting corporate R&D into European regions builds local green technological capability, a live question for regional and industrial policy.

link:https://cdn.ceps.eu/2026/06/2026-08.reader_title: Why the EU's digital partnerships with Asian technology powers are underachieving
link:https://cdn.ceps.eu/2026/06/2026-08.reader_what: Analysis finds partnerships fragmented across institutions and lacking any overarching coordination mechanism or legal architecture.
link:https://cdn.ceps.eu/2026/06/2026-08.reader_more: The report assesses partnerships pursued under the EU's 2025 International Digital Strategy with Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan, covering artificial intelligence, semiconductors, 6G and cybersecurity. Its diagnosis is institutional: many actors with overlapping but misaligned interests, spanning EU bodies, member states, partner ministries, industry and civil society, plus wide variation in depth, from South Korea's full Digital Partnership and Horizon Europe association status to Taiwan's informal channels. Being like-minded, the authors argue, does not guarantee aligned interests, and the stated move from a hub-and-spoke model to a network approach remains aspirational. They recommend widening engagement to smaller firms, start-ups, labour organisations and civil society, and building sectoral groupings among smaller sets of partners.

deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Policy analysis of EU digital partnership instruments and partner-country arrangements under the 2025 International Digital Strategy; report PDF supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Assessment and recommendation rather than empirical evaluation; the network model is described as aspirational and the proposed remedies are untested.

link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s43253-026-.reader_title: Why Europe's weaker economies have not moved into more technologically complex industries
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s43253-026-.reader_what: Sectoral analysis finds peripheral EU economies' industrial mix did not shift toward complex activities, 1995-2020.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s43253-026-.reader_why: Supports the case that industrial policy must target weaker economies' sectoral composition directly.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s43253-026-.reader_more: The authors build an index of technological complexity for each economic sector, then use econometric methods to relate sectoral investment to complexity, consumption, interest rates and foreign direct investment across EU countries from 1995 to 2020. Their reading is that divergence inside the Union is structural: an export-led growth model in the north and a credit-supported consumption model in the south left peripheral economies investing in less complex activities, which the authors connect to the break-up of industrial sectors in weaker member states. The complexity index is their own construction, so the results depend on how it is built. The analysis establishes patterns and associations across countries and sectors rather than proving a single cause of divergence.

deep_analysis.research_question: Why have technological and productive disparities widened between EU member states, and what role did sectoral investment play?
deep_analysis.main_finding: The sectoral composition of peripheral EU economies did not shift toward more technologically complex activities over 1995-2020, which the authors link to industrial disintegration in weaker economies and to the need for a redesigned industrial policy.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Author-constructed sectoral technological complexity index combined with econometric analysis of investment, consumption, interest rates and FDI, EU sectors 1995-2020; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Findings depend on the construction of the complexity index; the econometrics establish associations across sectors and countries rather than demonstrating causation, and the policy conclusion is the authors' argument.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Provides long-run evidence on intra-EU technological divergence directly relevant to European industrial and cohesion policy design.

link:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.giq.2026..reader_title: How the European Parliament told the story of AI while writing the AI Act
link:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.giq.2026..reader_what: Across 500 coded narratives, Parliament's framing of AI stayed stable from 2020 to 2024, even after ChatGPT.
link:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.giq.2026..reader_why: Documents the framings Parliament used while co-shaping the Act: control, risk-based regulation, joint approach.
link:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.giq.2026..reader_more: The Narrative Policy Framework breaks a policy story into four parts: characters, plot, setting and moral. The authors applied it to eighteen European Parliament documents from 2020 to 2024, manually coding 500 narratives, and found plots of control and of rising dominating, populated by heroes and beneficiaries rather than villains, presenting AI as both manageable and beneficial. Settings were security, global competition and European legal norms, while the morals centred on risk-based regulation, ethical standards and calls for a joint approach. The striking result is how little changed across four years, including after the release of ChatGPT. The study describes how Parliament talked about AI, which is not the same as showing that this talk determined the legislation.

deep_analysis.research_question: How did Members of the European Parliament construct and evolve policy narratives on AI during the legislative process leading to the AI Act?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Parliamentary AI narratives showed remarkable stability from 2020 to 2024 despite external shocks including the release of ChatGPT, dominated by plots of control and rising with heroes and beneficiaries, settings of security, global competition and European legal norms, and morals of risk-based regulation, ethical standards and a joint European approach.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Narrative Policy Framework applied to a corpus of 18 European Parliament documents from 2020 to 2024 with 500 manually coded narratives. Package contained no source text; the full publisher abstract was recovered online and corroborated by the authors' own summary of the study.
deep_analysis.qualification: Analyses parliamentary discourse rather than legislative causation; the corpus is 18 documents and the coding, while systematic, is manual and interpretive. Interpretation here rests on the abstract rather than the full article.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Illuminates how the EU's co-legislator framed AI during the AI Act process, bearing on the discursive conditions shaping European AI governance.

link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s44464-026-.reader_title: What the EU's 2025 export control update means for quantum computing research
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s44464-026-.reader_what: Commentary argues the EU controlled cryogenic components and wafer probers without waiting for multilateral list agreement.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s44464-026-.reader_why: Licensing requirements could reroute European quantum collaborations, procurement and technology choices.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s44464-026-.reader_more: Dual-use rules govern goods with both civilian and military applications. The authors' point is procedural as much as technical: the September 2025 update applied uniform EU controls to frontier items such as cryogenic components and wafer probers without waiting for a formal list update from the Wassenaar Arrangement, the consensus forum that has long anchored this area. They read the move as a shift toward plurilateral control aligned with the United States, Japan and Australia. Consequences for research are set out as plausible trajectories, including consortia switching between qubit technologies to avoid licensing hurdles. This is legal commentary written soon after the change, so effects on collaboration and supply chains are anticipated rather than observed.

deep_analysis.research_question: How does the EU's 2025 dual-use regulation update affect quantum technology research, collaboration and supply chains?
deep_analysis.main_finding: By imposing uniform controls on quantum-relevant hardware ahead of multilateral consensus, the EU signalled a shift toward plurilateral export control governance that the authors expect to reshape research collaboration, procurement and technology pathways in quantum computing.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Legal and policy commentary on the September 2025 EU dual-use regulation update set against Wassenaar Arrangement practice and allied controls; publisher open-access text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Written close to the regulatory change; the consequences for collaboration, procurement and technology choice are projections, with illustrative scenarios rather than evidence of adaptation.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns how European export control policy directly conditions access to equipment needed for quantum research and advanced chip fabrication.

link:https://ecas.org/wp-content/uploads.reader_title: Researchers report that free movement in the European Research Area still breaks down in practice
link:https://ecas.org/wp-content/uploads.reader_what: A 62-person survey finds administrative burden and discriminatory hiring or eligibility rules are the most-cited barriers.
link:https://ecas.org/wp-content/uploads.reader_more: The Fifth Freedom means free movement of researchers, knowledge and research funding across the EU. Sixty-two researchers in eleven member states answered three open questions and one closed one, and about 89 per cent backed formal EU recognition of the freedom. Administrative barriers and discriminatory hiring or funding eligibility were each raised by roughly 48 per cent of respondents; non-recognition of qualifications followed at 33 per cent. Respondents gave costed examples, including sworn translation fees of two to three hundred euros per diploma. The authors describe the sample as a self-selected pilot, not statistically representative.

deep_analysis.main_finding: Respondents overwhelmingly support formal recognition of a Fifth Freedom, but report administrative burden, discriminatory eligibility rules and non-recognition of qualifications as persistent barriers.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Self-selected online call for input; 62 responses from 11 EU member states plus two non-EU, December 2025 to April 2026; three open and one closed question.
deep_analysis.qualification: Explicitly a self-selected pilot sample, not statistically representative; an advocacy organisation's call for input rather than a controlled study.

admission.reason: Primary evidence on barriers to researcher mobility inside the European Research Area, produced as input to the ERA Act; squarely European research-policy material.

legacy_versions.reader_title: Researchers report that free movement inside the European Research Area breaks down in practice
legacy_versions.reader_what: A 62-person survey finds administrative obstacles and discriminatory hiring or eligibility rules are the most-cited barriers.
legacy_versions.reader_why: Written as input to the European Research Area Act expected in late 2026.
legacy_versions.reader_more: The Fifth Freedom here means free and equal movement of researchers, open access to scientific knowledge, and research funding circulating across the EU. Sixty-two researchers in eleven member states answered three open questions and one closed one, and about 89 per cent backed formal EU recognition of the freedom. Administrative barriers and discriminatory hiring or funding eligibility were each raised by roughly 48 per cent of respondents, with non-recognition of qualifications next at 33 per cent and named as the most-demanded reform. Respondents supplied costed personal cases, including sworn translation fees of two to three hundred euros per diploma and foreign experience counted at half value in salary scales. The authors describe the sample as a self-selected pilot, not statistically representative.

deep_analysis.research_question: What concrete structural barriers do researchers encounter to free movement of researchers, knowledge and funding within the EU?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Rights that exist formally in EU law are described as systematically undermined at operational level by national administrations and universities; administrative burden and discriminatory hiring or eligibility rules dominate, and automatic EU-wide recognition of qualifications is the reform most demanded.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Self-selected survey of 62 researchers across 11 member states, December 2025 to April 2026, with 148 open-text responses thematically coded; report PDF supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Explicitly a pilot: the sample is small, self-selected and skewed toward Spanish and Danish respondents, so percentages rest on few responses and are not representative of EU researchers.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Produced as direct input to the forthcoming ERA Act and documents specific obstacles to researcher mobility in the European Research Area.

link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_title: Turning community visions for 2050 into weighted priorities that city planners can use
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_what: Tested in Chios and Vilnius, the method converts community scenarios into ranked criteria for formal planning.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_why: Addresses the gap between community climate visioning and formal administrative prioritisation in urban planning.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_more: The approach has three parts: workshops that build shared scenarios for city futures to 2050; the Analytic Hierarchy Process, a technique that turns pairwise comparisons into numerical weights for criteria chosen by stakeholders; and expert review to check technical feasibility. It was run in two deliberately contrasting Living Labs, the Greek island of Chios and the Lithuanian capital Vilnius. The authors report that the sequence does translate qualitative community narratives into structured, weighted data that fits formal planning cycles. What is demonstrated is that the process runs and produces usable outputs in two settings, not that resulting plans were adopted or that urban climate resilience improved. Two sites also limit how far the approach can be generalised.

deep_analysis.work_kind: peer-reviewed methods study with pilot application
deep_analysis.research_question: How can community-led visioning of climate-resilient urban futures be translated into prioritised inputs that formal city planning can absorb?
deep_analysis.main_finding: A three-stage participatory foresight framework combining co-creative 2050 scenario building, Analytic Hierarchy Process weighting and expert feedback successfully converted qualitative community narratives into structured weighted criteria in two contrasting European city contexts.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Multi-method participatory foresight deployed in two Living Labs (Chios, Greece and Vilnius, Lithuania), combining scenario workshops, AHP prioritisation and expert validation; publisher open-access full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Demonstrates that the method works and yields planning-ready outputs; it does not show adoption by administrations or any improvement in climate resilience, and rests on two sites.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Offers a transferable participatory foresight and anticipatory governance method tested in two European city contexts.

link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_title: Testing whether Europe's food policies add up to a coherent path to transformation
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_what: Analysis finds EU food policy internally incoherent, incremental farm policy reform insufficient, and just-transition governance underdeveloped.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_why: Assesses Common Agricultural Policy reform against European Environment Agency imaginaries for a sustainable 2050.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_more: The authors combine participatory foresight with two structured techniques: the X-curve, which sequences the decline of an old system against the rise of a new one, and morphological analysis, which tests whether policy options can be consistently combined. Two expert workshops plus desk research generated transition measures, which were clustered into ten governance dimensions and cross-checked for consistency, yielding four stylised policy mixes. Measured against these, existing EU policy sits closest to a mixed-approaches logic but lacks internal coherence. The judgement that incremental Common Agricultural Policy reform cannot deliver transformation follows from that structured comparison rather than from modelled outcomes. The authors note that fully sequenced roadmaps remain for later work, and the evidence base is two expert workshops.

deep_analysis.research_question: How can foresight and transition research be combined to design internally coherent policy mixes for European food system transformation, and how does current EU policy compare?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Four internally consistent policy mixes were derived; current EU policy most resembles a mixed-approaches logic but lacks internal coherence, incremental Common Agricultural Policy reform is judged insufficient for transformation, and just-transition governance is underdeveloped.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Participatory foresight with two expert workshops and desk research, combined with the X-curve transition model and morphological cross-consistency assessment, anchored on four European Environment Agency imaginaries for 2050; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Conclusions rest on expert workshop input and structured consistency assessment, not on modelled or observed policy outcomes; the authors state that fully sequenced roadmaps are left to future research.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Applies foresight methods to assess coherence of an existing major EU policy framework and identifies specific governance gaps.

link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-026-.reader_title: A backcasting study of how humanities research evaluation could work by 2040
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-026-.reader_what: Review and backcasting propose three transitions: from indices to impact, toward open science, and toward technology-shaped evaluation.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-026-.reader_more: Backcasting works backwards from a desired future state to the steps needed to reach it. The authors pair that technique with a scoping review of the literature to sketch humanities research evaluation in 2040, sorting what they find into transitions, requirements and constraints. The three transitions are a move from index-based counting toward impact, from siloed work toward open science, and from tools toward what they term technopoly, meaning evaluation increasingly shaped by technology. They then set out nine policies with twelve first-level and twenty-eight second-level actionable steps. These are recommendations derived from literature and structured reasoning rather than tested interventions, and no particular national system or funder is examined empirically.

deep_analysis.research_question: What approaches, policies, indicators and infrastructures could support a discipline-appropriate framework for evaluating humanities research by 2040?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Three transitions are identified for humanities research evaluation, from index to impact, from siloed practice to open science, and from tools to technology-shaped evaluation, supported by nine proposed policies and forty actionable steps.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Scoping review of the literature integrated with backcasting from a 2040 endpoint; publisher full text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Outputs are normative recommendations derived from literature, not empirical findings or tested measures; no specific national or institutional evaluation system is assessed.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Relevant to ongoing research assessment reform debates, though the study is not Europe-specific and makes no claim about European systems.

link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_title: Experts map what would have to change for a post-growth Europe to be feasible
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_what: Participants judge most current trends to block strong sustainability while identifying specific openings for intervention.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_why: Produces scenarios and futures statements for Europe under post-growth rather than growth assumptions.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_more: Post-growth covers economic models such as degrowth, doughnut economics and wellbeing economics that aim for development within planetary limits rather than expanding output. The method the authors call integral foresight combines a review of literature on possible futures with horizon scanning and scenario building, run as multiple online rounds among researchers, subject experts and futurists. The output is a filtered, refined and categorised set of futures statements spanning social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal, ethical and demographic dimensions, plus scenarios built on differing assumptions. The conclusions are expert expectations elicited through a structured process, not forecasts or evidence about what will occur. Participants were recruited for their engagement with post-growth and sustainability, which shapes the range of views represented.

deep_analysis.research_question: What trends, weak signals and pathways bear on the feasibility of post-growth futures for Europe?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Experts expect many current trends to obstruct strong sustainability in Europe, while judging that intervention points exist and that desirable post-growth alternatives remain reachable, notably through democratic stewardship of nature.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Integral foresight process combining post-growth and sustainable development literature with horizon scanning and scenario building across multiple online interactive rounds with researchers, experts and futurists; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Findings are structured expert expectations rather than forecasts or empirical results, and participants were selected for existing engagement with post-growth and sustainability topics.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Develops explicitly European future alternatives under post-growth assumptions, offering scenario material for European sustainability and economic policy debate.

link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_title: The same foresight methods do different institutional work in different governance systems
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_what: Comparative study concludes EU foresight functions as networked, anticipatory infrastructure rather than isolated forecasting techniques.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_why: Covers ESPAS, the Strategic Foresight Reports, the Better Regulation Toolbox and Open Strategic Autonomy.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_more: The argument is that a method is never institutionally neutral: the same scenario or expert exercise does different work depending on the governance setting it sits in. The authors distinguish technocratic, market-managerial, networked and anticipatory logics, and map functions onto each, from expert prioritisation in the first to strategic positioning in the second, stakeholder alignment and legitimacy in the third, and early warning and policy adaptation in the fourth. The EU is the focal case, with Japan and South Korea used as deliberate contrasts rather than as a symmetrical comparison. Evidence comes from bibliometric mapping of Scopus, semantic analysis of method terms and manual validation of 68 publications, so the study characterises how foresight is positioned rather than measuring its influence on decisions.

deep_analysis.work_kind: peer-reviewed comparative conceptual and bibliometric study
deep_analysis.research_question: How do foresight methods perform different institutional functions across different governance logics, and where does EU strategic foresight sit?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Foresight methods are not institutionally neutral: their function shifts across technocratic, market-managerial, networked and anticipatory settings, and the EU shows the most developed combination of networked and anticipatory functions, making its foresight a governance infrastructure rather than a set of forecasting techniques.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Contrastive case design with the EU as focal case and Japan and South Korea as contrasts, combining exploratory Scopus bibliometrics, VOSviewer semantic analysis, manual validation of 68 publications and qualitative interpretation; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Deliberately asymmetric comparison based on literature and documents; it characterises institutional framing and does not measure whether foresight changed decisions or outcomes.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Maps the EU's own strategic foresight machinery, including ESPAS, Strategic Foresight Reports and the Better Regulation Toolbox, as an integrated governance capability.

link:https://doi.org/10.1017/pds.2026.10.reader_title: A proposed software architecture to make scenario planning practical for smaller companies
link:https://doi.org/10.1017/pds.2026.10.reader_what: Design paper proposes a modular AI-assisted scenario pipeline with guided wizard and shared knowledge backbone.
link:https://doi.org/10.1017/pds.2026.10.reader_more: Scenario management means building and maintaining alternative pictures of the future in order to test strategy against them. The authors start from the observation that smaller firms rarely have the time, expertise or tooling to do this well, and that available tools are fragmented. Their proposal pairs a guided wizard for non-specialists with a fuller environment for experienced users, both drawing on a shared knowledge store so that one exercise can feed later ones instead of ending as a standalone project. Recording where each input came from and keeping a person in the loop are intended to preserve explainability and human judgement. This is an architectural proposal presented at a design conference; it has not been implemented with firms or evaluated against outcomes.

deep_analysis.research_question: How can scenario management be made feasible for small and medium-sized enterprises that lack time, expertise and integrated tools?
deep_analysis.main_finding: The authors propose a modular, provenance-aware and AI-enabled foresight pipeline combining a guided wizard and an expert environment on a shared knowledge backbone, intended to turn one-off scenario projects into reusable organisational knowledge while keeping humans in the loop.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Conceptual architecture and design pattern description; publisher abstract and paper text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: A proposal only: no implementation, user trial or evaluation with enterprises is reported, so claimed reductions in effort and improvements in reuse are design intentions.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns foresight capability in smaller firms and the use of AI in scenario methods, though the paper makes no specifically European claim.

link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40804-025-.reader_title: Building a regulatory culture that anticipates innovation instead of chasing it
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40804-025-.reader_what: Article argues foresight, policy labs, pilot regulation and sandboxes should be integrated into one regulatory toolbox.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40804-025-.reader_why: Examines regulatory sandboxes as an EU policy tool, including their use in the AI Act.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40804-025-.reader_more: Regulatory lag is the gap between technology moving and law catching up. The author's case is that the remedy is not a single well-crafted statute but a standing capability: strategic foresight, iterative policy development, and learning from controlled trials. She surveys instruments already in use, including policy labs that develop rules with those affected, pilot regulation, experimentation and regulatory sandboxes in which firms test products under supervision, and argues they remain scattered rather than assembled into a coherent toolbox. The sandbox provisions of the EU AI Act are examined as the leading example. This is a legal and policy argument, so the claim that integration would improve regulation is reasoned rather than shown through evaluation.

deep_analysis.research_question: What does building an agile but robust anticipatory governance culture for regulating technological innovation involve?
deep_analysis.main_finding: A range of anticipatory instruments, including regulatory foresight, iterative policy development, policy labs, pilot regulation and sandboxes, are already used inventively but in isolation; the author argues they should be integrated systemically into jurisdictions' regulatory toolboxes rather than pursued as one-off fixes.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Doctrinal and policy analysis surveying anticipatory regulatory instruments, with attention to EU sandbox practice including the AI Act; publisher open-access full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Normative legal argument rather than empirical evaluation; no evidence is presented that integrating these tools improves regulatory outcomes.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Addresses how the EU regulates emerging technology and situates AI Act sandboxes within a wider anticipatory governance approach.

link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-024-.reader_title: Borrowing from deliberative democracy and philosophy of science to give foresight epistemic standing
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-024-.reader_what: Article argues reason-giving deliberation and perspectival realism can ground foresight's authority alongside established scientific disciplines.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-024-.reader_why: Addresses why foresight struggles for epistemic authority when set against established disciplines in policymaking.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-024-.reader_more: Perspectival realism is a position in philosophy of science holding that knowledge advances through interaction between distinct epistemic communities, each working with its own models. The author borrows it to argue that foresight produces what he calls modal models, structured accounts of what is possible, which can legitimately sit alongside other forms of evidence in policy. From deliberative democracy he takes the emphasis on pluralism and on giving reasons, presenting this as what lends foresight depth in public debate rather than merely generating options. The paper is a theoretical contribution: it offers a justification for foresight's standing in the policy process rather than evidence that adopting this framing changes practice.

deep_analysis.research_question: How can foresight establish epistemic authority in public policy alongside the natural and social sciences?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Deliberative democracy supplies an account of how reason-giving adds epistemic depth to foresight, while perspectival realism recasts foresight's outputs as modal models produced by an epistemic community, together offering a basis for foresight's standing in evidence-based policymaking.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Conceptual argument drawing on political theory and philosophy of science; publisher open-access full text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Theoretical and normative; no empirical test of whether this framing improves foresight's uptake or influence in policy processes.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns the credibility of foresight as an input to public policy, a standing question for institutionalised foresight, though not EU-specific.

link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40309-016-.reader_title: Using functional analysis and text mining to identify emerging technologies
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40309-016-.reader_what: Paper proposes analysing what a technology does, rather than what it is called, to detect emerging technologies.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40309-016-.reader_why: Authors argue the approach makes technology foresight affordable for small and medium-sized firms.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40309-016-.reader_more: Functional analysis asks what function an artefact performs for a user, instead of describing it by its components or its label. The authors apply that lens to technology foresight, combining it with natural language processing tuned for patent documents and with expert domain knowledge. They use it to look for development patterns, spot missing elements and potential failure points, and to strengthen conventional bibliometric approaches such as S-curve analysis. Their affordability argument rests on patent and publication data being cheap and widely available, so the constraint is analytical capacity rather than access. This is a 2016 methodological proposal demonstrated by its own authors, and the text-mining techniques available have changed substantially since.

deep_analysis.research_question: Can functional analysis, combined with text mining of patents, provide a cheaper and more user-centred way to identify emerging technologies?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Applying functional analysis to technology foresight, integrated with a patent-tailored natural language processing toolchain and expert knowledge, is proposed as a way to detect development patterns and emerging technologies while lowering cost enough for smaller firms to use.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Methodological development combining functional analysis, bibliometric S-curve analysis and NLP applied to patent documents, with illustrative application; publisher open-access full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Proposal demonstrated by its own authors without independent validation or benchmarking against alternative methods; published in 2016, so the text-mining component predates current techniques.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Offers a technology foresight method for identifying emerging technologies, with an explicit claim about accessibility for smaller firms.

link:https://demoshelsinki.fi/tag/public.reader_what: Topic index gathering Demos Helsinki pieces claiming EU mission governance is now tested and transferable.

link:https://demoshelsinki.fi/tag/public.reader_more: This record points to a tag archive page rather than a single publication. It lists short teasers for recent Demos Helsinki outputs on governance, wellbeing, economic growth and artificial intelligence. The newest item, from July 2026, draws on almost five years of the EU Cities Mission and argues, with Dark Matter Labs and the Mission Board, that mission governance has reached policy readiness. Related teasers argue that cities generate governing capacity Europe should build into a revised multilevel governance architecture. Other entries cover lessons from Finland pandemic crisis governance and a framework for democratic artificial intelligence governance for 2026 to 2028. No single research finding is presented on the page.

link:https://doi.org/10.1111/bioe.70159.reader_title: When can the social value of health data research justify weaker consent?
link:https://doi.org/10.1111/bioe.70159.reader_what: Argues weaker consent standards require genuine involvement and control for people whose health data is used.
link:https://doi.org/10.1111/bioe.70159.reader_why: Sets an ethical condition for opt-out data reuse under the European Health Data Space.
link:https://doi.org/10.1111/bioe.70159.reader_more: Data-intensive health research strains traditional informed consent because of the number of contributors and data points, open-ended questions and repeated or secondary use. The paper examines three distinct roles claimed for social value: preventing research waste and setting priorities, justifying risk to participants, and lowering consent standards. The authors argue that if social value is invoked to justify lower consent standards, then meaningful involvement and control must be available to data contributors or their representatives. The argument is conceptual rather than empirical and is set against moves towards opt-out systems, including in the European Health Data Space.

deep_analysis.research_question: What roles the concept of social value can legitimately play in justifying consent standards for data-intensive health research.
deep_analysis.main_finding: Social value cannot on its own justify lowering consent standards; doing so requires an appropriate form of meaningful involvement and control for data contributors.

link:https://doi.org/10.1111/1758-5899.7.reader_title: How the EU reconciled its openness and digital sovereignty stories
link:https://doi.org/10.1111/1758-5899.7.reader_what: Traces how EU digital connectivity and digital sovereignty narratives converged under rising geopolitical competition.
link:https://doi.org/10.1111/1758-5899.7.reader_why: Explains how Europe justifies both open digital partnerships and reduced dependence on foreign technology.
link:https://doi.org/10.1111/1758-5899.7.reader_more: The article studies the stories the European Union tells about governing digital technology, using the strategic narratives approach.
